title: TB7-13856
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The Appellants, XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and her adult son XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant) are citizens of China and appeal the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated June 29, 2017, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: The Appellants, XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and her adult son XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant) are citizens of China and appeal the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated June 29, 2017, rejecting their claims for refugee protection. The Appellants ask that the Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) substitute a finding that they are Convention refugee or a person in need of protection or refer the matter for redetermination.1 DETERMINATION

Pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA),2 I am setting aside the decision of the RPD and substituting it with my own. Specifically, on the evidence before me, I find that the Appellants are Convention refugees as they face a serious possibility of persecution in China.

The Appellants fear returning to China as they believe they will be harmed by the Chinese authorities, specifically the Family Planning Officials (FPO) and the Public Security Bureau (PSB). The Principal Appellant already had two children, including the Associate Appellant, when she learned in XXXX 2015 she was once again pregnant. At the hospital she was forced to abort the pregnancy despite her and her husband wanting to have the child. She was released from the hospital and scheduled to have a sterilization procedure approximately one week later. However, in order to avoid the procedure, the Principal Appellant and her husband went into hiding as both were concerned about being sterilized. After missing her sterilization appointment, the local FPO and PSB authorities visited their residence looking for the Principal Appellant and when they could not locate her, threatened the Associate Appellant to reveal her whereabouts. He expressed his opposition to the family planning policies in China and argued with the officials. Concerned he may be arrested and harmed, he also went into hiding. With the help of a smuggler, he came to Canada in XXXX 2015 followed by his mother about XXXX days later.

My role is to conduct an independent assessment of the evidence and review the RPD decision on a standard of correctness. The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony, which in some cases attracts deference. Unless specifically stated below, I have applied a correctness standard.3 PROCEDURAL HISTORY & APPROACH TO APPEAL

The Appellants refugee claim was heard by the RPD on June 22, 2017. The Appellants claim was rejected on June 29, 2017, at which time they appealed the decision to the RAD. The RAD upheld the rejection of their claims at which point the Appellants sought and were granted leave for judicial review at the Federal Court on October 16, 2018.

By way of a decision dated October 21, 2019, Justice Elliott granted the judicial review application based on a procedural fairness error by the RAD and set the decision aside.4 Justice Elliot ordered the matter be referred for redetermination by a different RAD panel. This is that appeal.

Along with the previous appeal record and memorandum, the Appellants submitted on January 18, 2021, a supplemental memorandum along with new evidence which I will address momentarily. For the purposes of this appeal, where applicable, I have considered the supplemental memorandum in addition to the original Appellants' memorandum.

The Appellants provided new evidence in their supplementary memorandum.5 Much of this evidence is not new but rather re-issued certificates of the exact evidence tendered before the RPD, the only difference being they have now been witnesses or attested to by a lawyer in China. For example, the Certificate of Diagnosis, Certificate of Abortion, and two notices of sterilization were all before the RPD.6 Additionally, the affidavit of a cousin, XXXX XXXX XXXX is essentially the same that was in evidence at the RPD.

Other pieces of evidence, such as an affidavit from the Principal Appellant's husband and Associate Appellant's father, XXXX XXXX, provides more details than the previous letter from him that was before the RPD, and the Appellants provide affidavits from two neighbour and communications with XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX. in Canada, evidence not before the RPD.7

In order to admit new evidence pursuant to subsection 110(4) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA), I must be satisfied that the new evidence arose after the RPD rejected the claim, or that it was either not reasonably available or the Appellants could not have been reasonably expected, in the circumstances, to present the evidence at the time of the rejection of the claim by the RPD.8 If the new evidence passes this initial step, I am then required to consider the factors set out in Raza9 and adopted in Singh10. These factors include the credibility, relevance, and newness of the evidence.

The Appellants correctly lay out the tests and requirements in order for new evidence to be admitted on appeal. However, they argue generally that the Appellants could not have reasonably been expected to present the evidence at the time of the rejection of their claim and that the evidence is relevant to the RAD's determination of their appeal.11

With the exception of the updated affidavit from the husband and father and the XXXX XXXX XXXX evidence, I find the Appellants could have reasonably been expected under the circumstances to provide all the evidence they seek to admit on appeal. In fact, as mentioned above, much of the evidence was indeed presented to the RPD and therefore was part of the record. Furthermore, the evidence from neighbours outlining what they overheard when the FPO and PSB officials came to the family home would potentially be highly relevant and the Appellants have failed to explain why such evidence was not reasonably available to them prior to the rejection of the claim.

Now, in respect to the affidavit of the husband concerning why there was a delay in claiming refugee by the Appellants and his prior refugee experience in Canada, along with the communication with XXXX XXXX XXXX, I do agree that the Appellants could not have been reasonably expected, in the circumstances, to present the evidence at the time of the rejection of the claim by the RPD as they could not have known the importance the RPD placed on this evidence, or the lack thereof, in its decision. Further, I agree that the evidence is relevant as it concerns one of the major findings of the RPD concerning a delay in claiming, is new as it provides details on the husband's refugee experience in Canada and the Appellants efforts in obtaining assistance in claiming refugee protection, and on its surface appears credible. While I reserve any determination as to the weight, if any, such evidence should receive, I do admit these two pieces of evidence.

The Appellant request that an oral hearing be held.12 Pursuant to subsection 110(6) of IRPA, the RAD may hold a hearing if there is documentary evidence referred to in subsection 110(3), which includes new evidence under subsection 110(4), and raises serious issues with respect to the credibility of the Appellants, is central to the decision with respect to the refugee protection claim, and if accepted would justify allowing or rejecting the claim. Otherwise, the RAD must proceed without a hearing, relying on the RPD record.

In this case, while I accepted some of the new evidence, I find that neither piece of evidence raises any serious credibility issues with respect to the Appellants as the evidence emanates from other sources. Further, while both pieces of evidence concern the delay in claiming in Canada, this issue was not determinative and even if I were to accept the Appellants' version of events, it would still not justify allowing or rejecting their claims. As such, an oral hearing is not warranted and will not be held.

The determinative issue for the RPD was credibility. The RPD made three significant findings that led to the rejection of the claim. Specifically, the RPD found the Appellants' evidence regarding their ability to depart China on their own passports was not credible and as a result the RPD found that they are not wanted by Chinese authorities, the Appellants' delay in claiming refugee protection in Canada undermined their subjective fear and credibility and finally, that the Appellants have failed to establish a religious or moral opposition to abortion.

The Appellants argue in their original memorandum that the RPD erred in each of the three specific findings, as well as the RPD treatment of the supporting documentary evidence. The detailed arguments of all these areas will be addressed shortly. Further, in the supplemental memorandum, in addition to the areas identified above, the Appellants argue that the RPD's findings were implausibility findings only to be made in the clearest of cases and not supported by the facts of this case. The Appellants also argue in respect to China's policy about having more than two children as well as the unavailability of an internal flight alternative, the latter of the arguments I dispose of as that was never an issue at the RPD and given the alleged agents of harm is the state consisting of Chinese authorities, an IFA would not be viable under the circumstances.

After my independent review of the evidence, for the reasons that follow, I find the RPD erred in each of the three areas identified by the Appellants, as well as its treatment of the supporting documentary evidence. Leaving China on Own Passports Credible and Plausible

The RPD drew a negative credibility inference from the Appellants ability to depart China on their own passports. After considering the steps taken by the Appellants with the assistance of a smuggler to first depart mainland China for Hong Kong and then onward to Canada, along with the available evidence of the Golden Shield and China's exit controls and the existence of official corruption, the RPD concluded that with the vast surveillance system in place, the Appellant's account of leaving on their own passports lacked credibility. Additionally, the RPD found that even if the Appellants were not yet wanted by officials, their use of their own passport to leave China would have been "recorded and relayed" to the local PSB who then would know the Appellants are not in China and would not look for them after their departure in XXXX 2015.13 Finally, noting the Appellants' evidence regarding the arrangements and steps taken by the smuggler through the exit checkpoints, the RPD doubted this was sufficient to evade China's exit controls in light of the general evidence in the National Documentation Package (NDP).

The Appellants argue that the RPD erred by overlooking the role that the smuggler played, as after all, they were hired to circumvent the exit systems in place, something that if they were unable to do successfully there would not be a lucrative smuggler business in existence. It is argued that because they were able to exit with a smuggler, their exit was unknown to the FPO and PSB and that is why they continued to look for the Appellants after they left China. Further, the Appellants argue the RPD speculates and suggests that the Golden Shield is foolproof which is not supported by the available evidence which indicates that individuals can avoid detection and procedures vary depending on the airport. Additionally, the Appellants point out that corruption, including bribery of officials, exists and it is not unreasonable to expect such corruption occurred in the Appellants case. Finally, the Appellants submit that in essence the finding of the RPD was one of implausibility and flawed in light of the available evidence.

Having independently reviewed the evidence, I agree with the Appellant that the RPD erred in respect to this particular issue. To be clear, while the RPD did make a credibility finding and preferred objective evidence in the NDP over the specific evidence of the Appellants, the finding was one of implausibility, even if that word was not specifically used. In essence, the RPD does not accept what the Appellants allege in terms of leaving China as plausible, in light of the country condition documents.

It must be noted that the courts have been clear in respect to implausibility findings, that they are to be made ...only in the clearest of cases, i.e., if the facts as presented are outside the realm of what could reasonably be expected, or where the documentary evidence demonstrates that the events could not have happened in the manner asserted by the claimant. A tribunal must be careful when rendering a decision based on a lack of plausibility because refugee claimants come from diverse cultures, and actions which appear implausible when judged from Canadian standards might be plausible when considered within the claimant's milieu.14 Additionally, the courts have commented that implausibility findings are ...inherently subjective assessments which are largely dependant on the individual Board member's perceptions of what constitutes rational behaviour. The appropriateness of a particular finding can therefore only be assessed if the Board's decision clearly identifies all of the facts which form the basis for their conclusions. The Board will therefore err when it fails to refer to relevant evidence which could potentially refute their conclusions of implausibility.15

The Appellants' evidence was clear in that the smuggler was specifically hired to ensure safe passage out of China despite the exit controls in place, this included arranging for visas, deciding when they would depart, entry into Hong Kong, and travel to the airport and onward to Canada.16 The Associate Appellant testified about what occurred at the Hong Kong border and that the smuggler went up first to speak to the immigration official in what the Associate Appellant believed to be a different language. Despite several questions inviting the Appellants to speculate as to how they could exit, they largely declined to do so indicating they did not know and that is why the smuggler was hired. In my view, there is nothing in the Appellants sworn testimony that raises credibility issues. They were consistent and testified to what they knew or witnessed and were clear about the things they did not know or were unsure of.

In respect to the objective documentary evidence, the NDP contains evidence from approximately one year prior to the Appellants' departure that indicates it is possible for individuals who are actually wanted by the PSB to nevertheless exit China, whether through errors or with the assistance of others, and those who were stopped from departing were often of a high profile.17 In this case, there is no evidence the Appellants had even been sought by the PSB or FPO beyond at the local level or that they were of a high profile that would warrant particular scrutiny. In my view the RPD speculated, without a basis for doing so, that the "PSB made a note of the claimant' alleged violations which would have been updated on China's vast database about its citizenry".18 There is no evidence of the PSB doing so or taking any other formal legal actions, such as issuing a summons or warrant for the Appellants arrest, which if it were the case could perhaps lend credence to the RPD's speculation as to whether the Appellants would have been entered into the Golden Shield database.

Furthermore, the objective documentary evidence reveals that "[c]orruption at every level was widespread"19 and "[c]orruption remained rampant, and many cases of corruption involved areas heavily regulated by the government".20 Customs and immigration officials were not immune to such activities, as the Appellants' documentary evidence reveals they too worked with smugglers and took bribes to smuggle individuals over a span of five years across the very same border, Shenzhen to Hong Kong, that the Appellants used to cross with the help of smuggler.21

Finally, the RPD again speculated that if the Appellants' passports were scanned and stamped then the PSB would know they are no longer in China and therefore not look for them. However, the Associate Appellant testified that he did not think his passport was scanned and perhaps the PSB did not know he had left the country and that is why they continued to look for him.22 Although equally speculative, this is a reasonable explanation in light of the RPD's concerns and could explain the PSB's pursuit of the Appellants after they had left the country.

Against this backdrop, after my independent assessment of the evidence, including the Appellants' testimony and the country documents, I find that it would not be implausible for the Appellants to leave China on their own passports with the use of a smuggler, regardless of whether they were indeed "wanted" by the FPO or PSB or not. The Appellants utilized the smuggler for this specific purpose and the smuggler handled all the arrangements for departure, with the Appellants following his directions. Furthermore, while I acknowledge that the Chinese government utilizes extensive surveillance measures to control who leaves the country, like with any system, failures do occur, whether unintentional or intentional through smugglers and corrupt officials.

For the above reasons, I find that it is plausible for the Appellants to have departed China on their own passports and with the assistance of a smuggler. As such, I make no negative credibility findings associated with this aspect of the Appellants claims. Delay in Making Refugee Claim in Canada

The RPD considered both Appellants' arrival in Canada in approximately mid XXXX 2015 and noted they had not filed for refugee protection until mid-XXXX 2015, a period of some XXXX months. The RPD rejected the Appellants' explanations that they were awaiting the arrival of the Principal Appellant's husband and Associate Appellant's father as neither credible nor reasonable as he would have been ineligible to pursue a claim given he had previously made one in Canada and it was refused. The RPD found that the Appellants' evidence about them not knowing this lacked credibility as the husband and father had legal counsel and it would have been reasonable to expect his counsel or immigration officials to have informed him of this ineligibility. Also, he spoke to the Appellants about his experiences and was involved in them coming to Canada. Furthermore, the RPD considered and rejected a further explanation from the Appellants that they were informed by an immigration consulting agency to wait for the husband and father as this would "raise serious issues of misconduct and negligence".23 Finally, the RPD drew a negative inference from the lack of any mention of this advice in the Appellants' Basis of Claim form and rejected their explanation that they did not think they had to include such details as they did explain in their BOC that the delay was to await for the husband and father. As a result, the RPD drew an adverse inference in respect to the Appellants' general credibility and found they failed to reasonably explain the four-months delay, indicating a lack of subjective fear.

The Appellants argue the RPD's findings that the husband would have been informed by his counsel or immigration officials that he is ineligible to make a second claim were speculative. Further, it is argued that the RPD erred by finding the omission of being informed by the initial consultant agency to wait for the husband to arrive, when in fact the Appellants did explain they were waiting for the husband and it was not necessary to mention who advised them to wait. Finally, the Appellants argue that a delay for claiming should not impugn their credibility if it has been reasonably explained as is the case here.
Having conducted my own independent assessment, I agree with the Appellants and find the RPD erred as alleged.

First, I agree that the RPD speculated not only as what the husband's lawyer or immigration official would have told him about making a second claim, the RPD also speculated that the husband, if he had known such information, would have told the Appellants. There was no evidentiary basis to support such speculation.

Secondly, I agree with the Appellants that there was no requirement for them to explain in their BOC who advised them to wait to make a claim as they explained they were waiting for the husband to arrive and to claim as a family, therefore explaining the why in their delay in claiming. I find this explanation of waiting for their husband and father to make a claim as reasonable, after all, he was the one who had previously resided in Canada and gone through the process himself, potentially being able to steer and guide them along the process. Further, when the Appellants realized that the husband could not be smuggled out of China, they initiated their refugee claims and they explained proactively in their BOC the reason for the delay in claiming.

Finally, I find that the Appellants' delay, while reasonably explained, was also quite short and at a time they had legal status in Canada. Perhaps if they had been arrested or without legal status and risked deportation and still waited to file for refugee protection, then a negative inference undermining their subjective fear would be appropriate. In these circumstances however, only being in the country for four months and waiting on a family member to arrive, I do not find the delay to be of any significance and certainly insufficient to be so egregious as to draw a negative inference in respect to the Appellants' general credibility.

I would also add that the new evidence regarding XXXX XXXX XXXX reveals that the firm exists and communication from them indicates that the Appellants went to see them in XXXX 2015. In my view, this evidence corroborates the Appellants claim that they met with someone from the agency and frankly there is no evidence to undermine their further claim that they were advised to wait for the husband and father to arrive to claim as a family.
As a result, I draw no negative inference in respect to the Appellants' four-month delay in claiming refugee protection upon arriving in Canada. Moral or Religious Opposition to Abortion

The RPD assessed the details surrounding the Principal Appellant's claim of being forced to have an abortion upon learning she was pregnant with her third child in XXXX 2015 and tied it to the husband's refused refugee claim years prior, finding the Appellants failed to establish they had a moral or religious opposition to the abortion. Specifically, the RPD seemed to take issue with the Appellants' evidence that their husband and father felt he was not given a fair hearing to establish his Christian beliefs and found that the refusal of his claim in 2007 was sufficient to doubt the husband's claims now that he opposed abortion due to his Christian faith. The RPD faulted the Appellants for what it described as "their collateral attack upon the correctness of the husband's prior refugee decision, failure to provide the husband's PIF, the reasons for decision, and his appeal decisions in the absence of a reasonable explanation".24 The RPD concluded that the Principal Appellant also failed to establish she was "opposed to abortion on moral grounds".25

The Appellants argue the RPD erred in finding that simply because the Principal Appellant's husband's and Associate Appellant's father's refugee claim as a Christian was refused that it means he was not truthful about opposing abortion. Further, the Appellants argue that the RPD erred as the Principal Appellant can oppose abortion independent of her husband's beliefs.

I find the RPD erred in its analysis of this issue. To begin with, there is no obligation on the Appellants to adduce their husband's or father's refugee documents. But even if they had, it is unclear to me what purpose this would serve. Perhaps the husband was a genuine Christian who failed to establish as much before the RPD, or perhaps he was not a genuine Christian at the time but had since turned to the faith. Or perhaps he was a genuine Christian who the RPD found could safely practice in China. The point is, none of this evidence was before the RPD and the RPD closed its mind off to the various possibilities that could be plausible.

However, more importantly, the RPD ignored the Principal Appellant's evidence that she opposed abortion. After all, even if her husband had no opinion on the subject, she was and is still free to decide how she felt and feels about the abortion and her evidence reveals that she was against the abortion, wanted to keep the baby, and felt the baby should not be harmed as it was "innocent". The RPD seems to dismiss this evidence solely on the basis of the husband's failed refugee claim. In my view this was an error and the Principal Appellant's evidence regarding her own beliefs about the abortion are reasonable and credible. As a result, I draw no negative inference from this evidence or issue.

In summary, I find the Appellants established that it was not implausible for them to exit China on their own passports and with the assistance of a smuggler, that the Principal Appellant opposed the abortion of her third child which she wanted to keep, and that the Appellants had a reasonable explanation for a relatively short delay in filing their refugee claim. Documentary Evidence in Support of the Claim

The RPD placed minimal weight on the Appellants' supporting documentary evidence as it was of the view that the Appellants were not generally credible, and this extended to their documentary evidence. The RPD noted that document fraud was prevalent in China and despite not making any explicit findings that the Appellants' documents were fraudulent, the RPD found that they did not overcome other credibility concerns.

The Appellants argue the RPD erred by generalizing that fraudulent documents are widely available without pointing to what was fraudulent about the Appellants' documents other than their general appearance. It is argued the documents are authentic.

After my independent analysis and given my findings above, I find the RPD erred by attributing little weight to the various documents they Appellants provided in support of their claim. Given that much of the RPD's analysis focused on the Appellants' general lack of credibility which I found to be an error, there is no basis to undermine the Appellants' documentary evidence. Although there is widespread document fraud in China, there is no basis for finding the particular documents of the Appellants are fraudulent. They appear to be issued by the appropriate authorities and in my view support an otherwise credible claim. The documents support the Principal Appellant's position that she was forced to undergo an abortion and then was scheduled for a sterilization procedure which she failed to attend. This was followed by a subsequent notice again for sterilization which she did not attend.

As a result, in my view, the documentary evidence supports the Appellants' position that the Principal Appellant was forced to undergo an abortion and is being sought for sterilization. Objective Documentary Evidence Regarding China's Family Planning Policies

I have considered the available documentary evidence regarding the treatment of women and families that oppose China's family planning policies. It is important to keep in mind that the Principal Appellant already has two children and when she was pregnant with her third child, the Chinese authorities forcibly terminated the pregnancy.

The objective evidence supports the Appellants' claim as it indicates that the Chinese "government restrict the rights of parents to choose the number of children they have" and used coercion and physical force to meet family planning goals, including aborting unauthorized pregnancies and forcing individuals to undergo sterilization procedures.26 Further, in respect to families with two children, such as the case here, the evidence indicates "one parent was often pressured to undergo sterilization",27 with reports of local officials including in Fujian province where the Appellants are from being encouraged to take whatever measures are necessary to enforce family planning policies.28 I note that the Appellants' evidence was entirely consistent with the objective evidence, as she was forced to undergo an abortion that she did not want after which she was scheduled for sterilization.

In terms of the Associate Appellant, I find his explicit opposition to China's family planning policies would be viewed as anti-government or anti-Chinese Communist Party and put him at risk of persecution based on his political opinions. It is noteworthy to point out that China is an "authoritarian state that systematically curbs fundamental rights, including freedom of expression, association and assembly when it is perceived to threaten the rule of the Chinese Communist Party (CCP)."29 Other sources report that "[i]ndividuals and groups regarded as politically sensitive by authorities faced tight restriction on their freedom to assemble, practice religion, and travel both within China and overseas. Authorities used extralegal measures, such as enforced disappearances and strict house arrest, to prevent public expression of critical opinions".30

I note the Associate Appellant's evidence was that government officials threatened him with consequences after he confronted them about China's family planning policies and stated that the government should not be involved in the right of people to give birth. Since then, the FPO have attended the family home along with the PSB looking for the Associate Appellant and requiring him to report to their office immediately.31

In light of the above evidence, I find the Principal Appellant faces a serious possibility of persecution as a member of a particular social group, that being, a woman who opposes abortion and faces sterilization due to her already having two children. As for the Associate Appellant, I find he faces a serious possibility of persecution due to his explicit political opposition to China's family planning policies and his expressed beliefs that it is not the role of the government to control how many children women should have.

The RAD, pursuant to paragraph 111(1)(b) of the IRPA, sets aside the decision of the RPD and substitutes a decision that the Appellants are Convention refugees.
